AI & Community Banks: Friends or Foes?

Practical AI, emerging risks, and the questions leaders should be asking

Chris Busse · SingleStone

Friends Foes

Act I

Friend or foe?

It’s the question in the title of this session. Let’s give it a fair hearing before we set it aside.

Friends Foes

Wrong question

Neither. It isn’t a person.

Friend and foe describe relationships, and AI can’t have one with your bank. It feels no loyalty and holds no grudge.

  • It is “an engineered or machine-based system that can, for a given set of objectives, generate outputs such as predictions, recommendations, or decisions.”[1]
  • A language model stitches together language it has seen “without any reference to meaning.”[2]
  • So it can be fluent and wrong at once. NIST’s word for it is confabulation.[3]
a model, not a mind
  1. NIST (2023). AI Risk Management Framework 1.0, NIST AI 100-1, p. 1 & §5.
  2. Bender, Gebru, McMillan-Major & Shmitchell (2021). On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots. FAccT ’21, p. 617.
  3. NIST (2024). Generative AI Profile, NIST AI 600-1, §2.

Not a foe

Most AI pilots don’t crash. They never leave the ground.

You’ve seen the headline: “95% of AI pilots fail.” Look under the cowling.

  • MIT’s own report puts the gap down to approach rather than model quality or regulation.[1]
  • What breaks is mechanical: brittle workflows, and nobody owning the result.[1]
  • RAND’s most common root cause: leadership “misunderstanding how to set the project on a pathway to success.”[2]

Treat the 95% with care. It comes from a small, preliminary, self-reported study.[1]

grounded pilot
  1. Challapally et al., MIT NANDA (Jul. 2025). The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 (preliminary findings).
  2. Ryseff, De Bruhl & Newberry, RAND (Aug. 2024). The Root Causes of Failure for AI Projects, RR-A2680-1.

But people can misuse it

The threat is whoever’s holding the tool.

  • FinCEN has seen “an increase in suspicious activity reporting … describing the suspected use of deepfake media in fraud schemes targeting their institutions and customers.”[1]
  • An Arup employee sent about US$25 million after a video call with deepfaked colleagues. Arup: “We can confirm that fake voices and images were used.”[2]
  • Deloitte projects generative AI could enable US fraud losses of $40 billion by 2027, up from $12.3 billion in 2023.[3]

Even here, the danger “comes not from the technology used to create it, but from people’s natural inclination to believe what they see.”[1]

Deepfake a person
  1. FinCEN (Nov. 13, 2024). Alert on Fraud Schemes Involving Deepfake Media Targeting Financial Institutions, FIN-2024-Alert004.
  2. Fortune (May 17, 2024). Arup confirms it was the victim of a HK$200M (US$25M) deepfake video-call fraud.
  3. Deloitte Center for Financial Services (May 29, 2024). Generative AI is expected to magnify the risk of deepfakes and other fraud in banking.

A tool can’t choose

A person decides, and a person answers for it.

“A computer can never be held accountable. Therefore a computer must never make a management decision.”[1]

  • Lawyers who filed ChatGPT’s invented cases were sanctioned: “existing rules impose a gatekeeping role on attorneys.”[2]
  • For banks, the agencies are blunt: “A banking organization has ultimate responsibility…”, whatever a vendor or an AI did.[3]

As then-FTC Chair Lina Khan put it in 2023, “There is no AI exemption to the laws on the books.”[4]

Approved by: a person

  2. Mata v. Avianca, Inc., No. 22-cv-1461 (PKC), 678 F. Supp. 3d 443 (S.D.N.Y. June 22, 2023).
  3. OCC, Fed, FDIC & NCUA (Sept. 15, 2026). Proposed Third-Party Risk Management Guidance, FR Doc. 2026-18859.
  4. FTC (Apr. 25, 2023). FTC Chair Khan and officials from DOJ, CFPB and EEOC release joint statement on AI.

Act II

Choosing the tool

Pick the job first, then the tool, then the controls.

But if we must keep the metaphor…

AI is the friend who has every tool.

It will sell your bank one off the shelf, or help you build your own.

Every tool.

Build some. Buy some. Match each one to a job.

  1. “Knolling”: coined 1987 by Andrew Kromelow in Frank Gehry’s shop; popularized by Tom Sachs.

The real risk

AI is easy to come by. Choosing it well is the hard part.

“I suppose it is tempting, if the only tool you have is a hammer, to treat everything as if it were a nail.”[1]

“Can AI do this?” will nearly always get a yes. The better question is which tool suits which job.

The tools are already in the building: 49% of banks say they have deployed generative AI.[2]

  1. Maslow, A. H. (1966). The Psychology of Science, pp. 15–16 (via Quote Investigator).
  2. Cornerstone Advisors (Jan. 29, 2026). What’s Going On in Banking 2026. n = 416 executives.

Practical applications

Start with the job, not the tool.

Three jobs AI does well at a community bank:

  • Efficiency. Loan-file intake, call and meeting summaries, first drafts of policies and procedures.
  • Customer service. After-hours answers, call routing, and an assistant at your front-line banker’s elbow.
  • Better decisions. Triage for fraud and BSA alerts, first drafts of credit memos, early warning across the portfolio.

AI for customer support is now a top opportunity for 47% of community bankers, up 16 points in a year.[1]

Efficiency Service Decisions
  1. CSBS (2025). 2025 CSBS Annual Survey of Community Banks, p. 17.

Finding the job

Walk the process before you pick the job.

Follow one loan file from application to close. Mark:

  • Waits. Where the file sits in a queue. The waiting usually dwarfs the work.[1]
  • Re-keying. The same data typed into a second system.
  • Rework. The file goes back for something missing.
  • Judgment. Where a person makes the call. AI can help, but the call stays with the person.

The job for AI is usually a handoff or a re-key, not the whole process.[2]

Apply Intake Underwrite Close Rework Re-key Longest wait
  1. Rother & Shook (1999). Learning to See: Value Stream Mapping to Add Value and Eliminate Muda. Lean Enterprise Institute.
  2. Challapally et al., MIT NANDA (Jul. 2025). The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 (preliminary findings).

Finding the job

Draw the walls: one job, one room.

Your bank already has walls: to deposits a customer is an account holder; to lending, a borrower; to BSA, a subject.[1] Give AI a job that fits in one:

  • One room. One owner, one vocabulary, and only that room’s data.
  • Through a door. At a handoff you’ve mapped, rather than reaching into every room.
  • Worth doing. High volume, a person already checking the work, and a clear measure of better.

Software designers call these bounded contexts.[2] Pilots that sprawl across rooms stall on tools that “integrate poorly.”[3]

Depositscustomer = depositor BSA / AMLcustomer = risk subject Lendingcustomer = borrower
  1. Fowler (Jan. 15, 2014). BoundedContext. martinfowler.com.
  2. Evans (2003). Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software. Addison-Wesley.
  3. Challapally et al., MIT NANDA (Jul. 2025). The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 (preliminary findings).

Build or buy

Your friend can sell you a tool, or help you make one.

AI made small tools cheap to build. It did not make them cheap to own.

  • Buy what every bank needs: core, fraud, document intake. Your diligence is the control.
  • Build what’s yours alone, and keep it small: an internal assistant, a workflow, a report. Then you’re the vendor, with the testing, change control and support that comes with it.

Lean toward buying: MIT found internal builds “fail twice as often.”[1] Most community banks already do.[2]

Build
  1. Challapally et al., MIT NANDA (Jul. 2025). The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 (preliminary findings).
  2. U.S. Treasury (Mar. 2024). Managing AI-Specific Cybersecurity Risks in the Financial Services Sector.

If you buy

Buying the tool doesn’t sell off the risk.

“Use of third parties does not diminish banks’ responsibility to manage risks.”[1] Ask the vendor:

  • Is our customers’ data used to train your models?
  • How will you tell us when the model changes?
  • Can we explain its output to an examiner?
  • How do we leave?

Your core’s AI roadmap is your AI roadmap. The September 2026 proposal comes with a joint statement on community banks and their core providers.[1]

Buy
  1. FDIC FIL-58-2026 (Sept. 11, 2026). Proposed Interagency TPRM Guidance; Joint Statement on Core Service Providers.

Show of hands

Raise your hand if your bank…

  1. has people using a chatbot at work, approved or not.
  2. has switched on an AI feature your core or a vendor shipped.
  3. is running an AI pilot right now.
  4. has built an AI tool of its own.

Keep it up if you could name the person who owns it.

If you’ve already started

Already started? Run it back through the plan.

Nobody needs to start over. Take stock of what’s already in the building.

  • Inventory. Every AI tool in use, including pilots, vendor features and personal accounts.
  • Map. Tie each one to a job and a room. If no one can say which, you’ve learned something.
  • Tier. Check that the controls match the risk.
  • Decide. Keep, fix or retire each one, and name an owner for every keeper.

The tools came in ahead of the plan: 78% of AI users bring their own to work, and 80% at small and mid-sized companies.[1] Retiring a pilot is a perfectly good outcome.

Keep Fix Retire
  1. Microsoft & LinkedIn (May 8, 2024). 2024 Work Trend Index Annual Report: AI at Work Is Here. Now Comes the Hard Part.

Emerging risks

Match the tool to the risk.

  • Pencil. Drafting and summarizing, with a person editing everything.
  • Drill. Customer-facing chat and copilots on internal data. You own what it says.[1]
  • Crane. Credit, fraud, BSA, pricing. These need validation, fair-lending testing, and adverse-action reasons that are “specific.”[2]

Built or bought, the tier follows the job. And the 2026 model-risk guidance puts generative and agentic AI out of scope,[3] so if you build one, designing those controls falls to you.

Low Medium High
  1. Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149 (B.C. Civil Resolution Tribunal, 2024).
  2. 12 CFR 1002.9(b)(2), Reg. B. (CFPB Circulars 2022-03 and 2023-03 were withdrawn May 12, 2025; the rule stands.)
  3. Fed SR 26-2 / OCC Bulletin 2026-13 (Apr. 17, 2026). Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management; supersedes SR 11-7.

Emerging risks

Every tool gets only the data its job needs.

The safeguards didn’t change when the tools did.[1]

  • Any tool. Keep an approved list, and keep customer information out of consumer AI and personal accounts.
  • Bought. Put it in the contract: no training on your data, retention you control, notice of a breach.
  • Built. You’re the custodian: the least data the job needs, with access controls and logs.
  • Every tool. Treat prompts and outputs as records.

And expect the fraud to come down-market, to “smaller institutions.”[2]

Customer data
  1. Interagency Guidelines Establishing Information Security Standards: 12 CFR 364 App. B (FDIC); 30 App. B (OCC); 208 App. D-2 (Fed).
  2. U.S. Treasury (Mar. 2024). Managing AI-Specific Cybersecurity Risks in the Financial Services Sector.

Governance

Keep a human in the cockpit.

“Loop thinking creates blame cultures. Cockpit thinking creates ownership cultures.”[1]

  • Inventory every AI tool, including the ones inside vendor products.
  • Give each one a named pilot, and report to the board.
  • A person decides anything that affects a customer.
  • Watch the gauges: re-test when the vendor changes the model.

Keep it proportionate. The OCC says its guidance “does not … require community banks to perform annual model validation.”[2] Examiners oversee AI with the rules they already have.[3]

Human in the cockpit
  1. Mishra, T. (n.d.). Time to retire “human-in-the-loop” and embrace “human-in-the-cockpit.” SingleStone.
  2. OCC Bulletin 2025-26 (Oct. 6, 2025). Model Risk Management: Clarification for Community Banks.
  3. GAO (May 2025). Artificial Intelligence: Use and Oversight in Financial Services, GAO-25-107197.

Act III

What comes next

Lessons from working with dozens of executives and their companies. They all lead to the same place.

What comes next

Everything in the AI industry has a six-month shelf life.

  • Revisit. Decisions made six months ago were made on old facts.
  • Re-test. Something that didn’t work last spring may work now.
  • Date it. Put a review date on every AI decision.

The length of task AI can finish on its own has doubled about every seven months since 2019.[1]

October Six months
  1. Kwa, West, Becker et al., METR (Mar. 18, 2025). Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks. arXiv:2503.14499.

What comes next

There’s no magic wand in the chest, and you’ll likely buy AI more than once.

  • The market is messy. Gartner counts about 130 real agentic-AI vendors among the thousands claiming the label.[1]
  • It keeps moving. Expect to re-buy, re-contract and re-test as models and vendors change.
  • Buy the exit. Make sure you can take your data with you and leave on reasonable terms.

Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be canceled by the end of 2027.[1]

  1. Gartner (Jun. 25, 2025). Gartner Predicts Over 40% of Agentic AI Projects Will Be Canceled by End of 2027.

What comes next

You won’t know your new normal until you’re living in it.

No one planning a transformation really knows what the new operating reality will look like.

  • Small. Take steps you can finish in a quarter.
  • Reversible. Favor pilots, short terms and data you can take back.
  • Measured. Agree up front what “better” means, so you’ll recognize it when it arrives.
? ?

What comes next

The slop is rising inside your own walls.

AI-written memos, decks and replies that look finished and say nothing.

  • It moves the work. The sender saves time, and the reader spends it: nearly two hours apiece.[1]
  • It costs trust. Every obviously machine-written memo makes the next one harder to take seriously.
  • The fix is a norm. Whoever sends it stands behind it, and says when AI wrote the draft.

40% of U.S. employees received “workslop” in the past month.[1] Merriam-Webster’s 2025 word of the year: slop.[2]

Workslop
  1. Niederhoffer, Kellerman, Lee, Liebscher, Rapuano & Hancock (Sept. 22, 2025). AI-Generated “Workslop” Is Destroying Productivity. Harvard Business Review.
  2. Merriam-Webster (Dec. 2025). Word of the Year 2025: slop.

What comes next

The bad guys are ahead of us.

Fraud rings, ransomware crews, scammers, insiders, hostile states. None of them waits for a committee, a contract or an examiner.

  • They move first. A new capability reaches them long before it clears your procurement.
  • They come down-market. Treasury expects them to move toward “more vulnerable corners of the sector like smaller institutions.”[1]
  • It’s working. Reported internet-crime losses reached $16.6 billion in 2024, up 33%.[2]

That’s why the controls in Act II matter, and why your defenses will need AI as well.

  1. U.S. Treasury (Mar. 2024). Managing AI-Specific Cybersecurity Risks in the Financial Services Sector.
  2. FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (Apr. 23, 2025). Internet Crime Report 2024.

What comes next

People are saying the quiet part out loud. So who trains the juniors?

“In the next few years, we expect that this will reduce our total corporate workforce.”[1]

  • The bottom rungs. Employment of 22–25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs is 19% below trend, mostly because fewer are being hired.[2]
  • Your bench. Today’s analysts, processors and tellers are tomorrow’s chief lender, BSA officer and COO.
  • Design the apprenticeship. If AI writes the first draft, have juniors check it, and teach them what they’re checking for.
Senior Entry level
  1. Jassy, Amazon (Jun. 17, 2025). Message from CEO Andy Jassy: Some thoughts on Generative AI.
  2. Brynjolfsson, Chandar & Chen, Stanford Digital Economy Lab (Aug. 2026 revision). Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence.

It’s the data

The first hard question comes on day one: why did it do that?

Someone will ask it early: an examiner, a customer, or a member of your board.

  • What it saw. The inputs, and the data behind them.
  • What it said. The output, and what a person did with it.
  • Which version. The model, the prompt and the settings on that date.
  • Who approved it. The owner, and the decision on record.

Reg B still wants “specific” reasons for a denial.[1] Whatever you don’t record at launch, you can’t explain later.

Saw Said Version Approved
  1. 12 CFR 1002.9(b)(2), Reg. B. (CFPB Circulars 2022-03 and 2023-03 were withdrawn May 12, 2025; the rule stands.)

It’s the data

Most of your AI governance answers are already in your data governance.

  • What does it see? Classification and access.
  • Where did that come from? Lineage.
  • Is it right? Data quality.
  • How long do we keep it? Retention.
  • Who answers for it? The data owner.

RAND’s second root cause of failed AI projects: the data isn’t there.[1] Gartner expects 60% of AI projects without AI-ready data to be abandoned.[2]

AI governance Data governance Sees? Source? Right? Keep? Who? Owners Access Retention Lineage Quality

  2. Gartner (Feb. 26, 2025). Lack of AI-Ready Data Puts AI Projects at Risk.

It’s the data

And doing AI governance will improve your data governance.

Every AI tool you roll out puts your data to the test.

  • It finds the gaps. The stale field, the missing owner, the spreadsheet nobody documented.
  • It forces decisions. Who may see what, for how long, and why.
  • It pays twice. Fix the data for the AI, and every report, model and exam that relies on it improves too.

63% of organizations don’t have, or aren’t sure they have, the data management practices AI needs.[1]

AI Data
  1. Gartner (Feb. 26, 2025). Lack of AI-Ready Data Puts AI Projects at Risk.

Act III

It’s the data.

Working with AI is mostly about working with your data, and doing it right.

For the board table

Five questions leaders should be asking.

  1. Which jobs are we giving AI? Have we walked the process, and who gets hurt if it goes wrong?
  2. Is this the lightest tool that does the job?
  3. Are we building or buying, and what do our vendors and our core do with our customers’ data?
  4. Could we explain the result to a customer and to an examiner?
  5. Who owns each AI tool, and do we know what data it sees and keeps?
